questions.q: Why does Taleb say life is not linear?
a: Some outcomes are path-dependent, so a restart would end differently
Consistent effort always produces proportional rewards
Luck evens itself out over a long enough lifetime
Skill matters far more than timing in most fields
questions.why: The first lesson explains path dependence and says a single extra step can suddenly trigger a huge reward.

questions.q: What does the QWERTY keyboard example illustrate?
a: A standard can lock in after a tipping point even if it isn't ideal
Good design always wins out over time
Early inventions rarely survive competition
Practice makes any awkward tool feel natural
questions.why: The summary notes QWERTY persisted because switching would be a hassle, not because it was the best layout.

questions.q: Why does the summary argue we need our irrational emotions?
a: They help us decide when reason alone cannot choose
They make us more persuasive to other people
They protect us from taking any kind of risk
They sharpen our memory of past events
questions.why: The second lesson compares emotions to a coin flip that ends deliberation when outcomes are truly indifferent.

questions.q: What does the parable of Buridan's donkey show about purely rational choice?
a: It can leave us stuck and unable to act at all
Animals act on instinct rather than thought
Hunger always outweighs thirst in animals
Random choices are usually worse than planned ones
questions.why: The donkey starves between equal options, illustrating why a little randomness helps us stop deliberating.

questions.q: How does Taleb suggest we handle the harmful kind of randomness?
a: With a Stoic attitude and responsibility for our own behavior
By avoiding every decision that carries any risk
By trusting expert forecasts more carefully
By treating all outcomes as equally likely
questions.why: The third lesson says Stoicism means meeting random blows with elegance, without blame or complaint.
